nodes.label: Bug: Failover Proxy `then` Trap Made Ports Look Thenable
nodes.rationale: The proxy synthesized a callable for every property including `then`, so NestJS DI awaited the port as if it were a promise. Fixed with an anyProviderImplements() allowlist so only real port methods are synthesized.
nodes.norm_label: bug: failover proxy `then` trap made ports look thenable

nodes.label: OTLP Traces/Metrics/Logs Pipelines
nodes.rationale: Applications speak OTLP to the collector and nothing else, so moving to a managed observability backend later is an exporter change in this file rather than a code change anywhere in the monorepo.

nodes.label: Multi-Provider Registry + Failover Chain
nodes.rationale: Payment, identity, FX and SMS are multi-provider by default behind one port, so adding a provider means one adapter plus one registry entry and nothing else.

nodes.label: Port Proxy Chain (cache → breaker → retry → timeout → instrumentation → adapter)
nodes.rationale: Every outbound third-party call goes through a port and every port is wrapped in the same decorator chain, so resilience and observability are structural rather than per-call discipline. Calling an SDK or fetch directly from a service bypasses all of it.
nodes.norm_label: port proxy chain (cache → breaker → retry → timeout → instrumentation → adapter)

nodes.label: GET /admin/providers — Provider Health and Circuit-Breaker State
nodes.norm_label: get /admin/providers — provider health and circuit-breaker state

nodes.label: Bug: Fastify Rejected Empty JSON Bodies
nodes.rationale: Fixed on both sides: a custom content-type parser in the API accepts an empty body, and the web client only sets content-type when a body actually exists.
nodes.norm_label: bug: fastify rejected empty json bodies

nodes.label: @xb/contracts Zod Schemas as Single Source of Truth
nodes.rationale: Request/response validation, generated types and the frontend client all derive from the same Zod schemas, so front end and back end cannot drift.
nodes.norm_label: @xb/contracts zod schemas as single source of truth

nodes.label: Deviation 3: Back Office in Next.js, Not React+Vite
nodes.rationale: One toolchain and one generated API client across both surfaces beats a second bundler and a second client for a data-dense internal tool.
nodes.norm_label: deviation 3: back office in next.js, not react+vite

nodes.label: BUILD: Last-Mile Provider Abstraction
nodes.rationale: Follows the same pattern as the FX and store-adapter ports so the system can pick AloPeyk vs Snapp Box vs pickup point vs traveler per order on cost, SLA and coverage.

nodes.label: Modular Monolith (not microservices)
nodes.rationale: One deployable with strict internal module boundaries plus an in-process event bus gives DDD separation without distributed-systems overhead at MVP scale. Because modules already talk via events and interfaces, any module can later be extracted into a service without rewriting callers.

nodes.label: Ports & Adapters (Hexagonal) Architecture
nodes.rationale: Three dependencies are gated outside the team's control (foreign payment/banking, procurement method, logistics+customs). Putting each behind an interface with a stub adapter lets the core and both surfaces be fully functional before any gate clears, and lets the real provider be swapped in with zero core rework. The gates decide WHICH adapter goes live, never WHETHER the system works.

nodes.label: Escrow + Reputation Trust Rails
nodes.rationale: Copied from Grabr and hawala networks: money released only on verified delivery or scan, plus agent/traveler ratings, verification and limits. Built once and reused across travelers, agent gates and pickup points.

nodes.label: Model C: Crowdshipping / Traveler Network
nodes.rationale: Scored 3/5 — a supplementary channel, never the backbone. Capacity is lumpy, liability and authenticity risk are real, and customs exposure (personal-import limits, undeclared goods) is the sharp edge. Confined to Leg B for value-dense items with escrow released on hub scan-in rather than personal handoff.

nodes.label: Business Line 3: Enterprise Import/Export Procurement Desk
nodes.rationale: Highest value per account but highest compliance and working-capital intensity, so it is deferred to phase 3+ and entered through the lowest-risk wedge (consolidation + tracking dashboard, or a single-category managed desk).
nodes.norm_label: business line 3: enterprise import/export procurement desk

nodes.label: Business Line 2: Merchant Fulfillment Platform
nodes.rationale: Instead of only competing with Iranian micro-retailers for end consumers, sell them the infrastructure — turning competitors into distribution and funding working capital through their prepaid wallets.

nodes.label: AloPeyk / Snapp Box (Iranian gig delivery fleets)
nodes.norm_label: alopeyk / snapp box (iranian gig delivery fleets)

nodes.label: Five-Leg Fulfillment Chain (A–D, points 1–5)
nodes.rationale: Naming legs and handoff points explicitly is what allows each leg to be priced separately, sold separately to merchants, and have its provider swapped independently.

nodes.label: Model A: Integrated Forwarder + Gig Last-Mile
nodes.rationale: Rated 5/5 for MVP: fastest to launch, asset-light, reuses mature infrastructure on both ends (UAE forwarders, Iranian gig fleets), cleanest compliance profile, and yields the unified tracking data that constitutes the moat.
nodes.norm_label: model a: integrated forwarder + gig last-mile

nodes.label: Model E: Own Warehouses + Own Fleet (deferred)
nodes.rationale: Best eventual unit cost and control, but heavy capex and slow to stand up — explicitly deferred to the scale phase and not built for MVP.
nodes.norm_label: model e: own warehouses + own fleet (deferred)

nodes.label: Route Feasibility Matrix (UAE / Turkey / Germany / UK)
nodes.norm_label: route feasibility matrix (uae / turkey / germany / uk)

nodes.label: Unified Multi-Leg Tracking Lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Carrier, warehouse and marketplace statuses are heterogeneous and unreadable to customers; normalizing them into one legible lifecycle is what turns observable execution into trust, and never leaks raw carrier statuses.

nodes.label: Prepaid Merchant Wallet Money Model
nodes.rationale: A merchant tops up in IRR and each order debits the balance, so there is zero credit risk and the merchant funds the working capital. Escrow-collected checkout is phase 2 and credit terms are strictly gated on an AI credit score.

nodes.label: One Engine, Three Demand Surfaces
nodes.rationale: B2C, merchant-B2B and enterprise import are three front-ends on one shared spine; everything hard and defensible (resolver, quote engine, FX, procurement, treasury, ledger, tracking, ops console, compliance allowlist) is built once, and the lines differ only in surface, policy and pricing. Three revenue lines amortize one build.

nodes.label: Wholesaler Mode vs Agent Mode
nodes.rationale: Agent mode exposes the full landed-cost breakdown and invites disintermediation; wholesaler mode quotes one delivered-to-Iran price with the source hidden and margin embedded. New merchants default to wholesaler mode, with agent-mode transparency unlocked only at higher tiers or volume commitments.

nodes.label: DECISION: Asset-Light (own orchestration, rent metal)
nodes.rationale: Own the orchestration and the data (which point, which leg, which provider, unified tracking) but rent the physical assets — forwarder warehouses, freight carriers, Iranian gig last-mile. Owning warehouses and fleet is a scale-phase decision, never an MVP one.

nodes.label: DECISION: Integrate Iranian Gig Fleets as Leg-D Providers
nodes.rationale: Domestic last-mile in Iran is already solved by AloPeyk, Snapp Box and Miare, so integrating them gives on-demand door delivery with zero capex. The genuinely novel gig layer is the cross-border traveler network, not the domestic one.
nodes.norm_label: decision: integrate iranian gig fleets as leg-d providers

nodes.label: Modular 'Sell Legs, Not Bundles' Merchant Toolkit
nodes.rationale: Packages run from full-to-door down to consolidation-only, each separately priced. Merchants who already have local last-mile buy exactly the expensive, hard part (source procurement, international leg, customs) and keep what they are good at — which is also what removes the 'thin middle' commoditization risk.
nodes.norm_label: modular 'sell legs, not bundles' merchant toolkit

nodes.label: DECISION: UAE (Dubai) → Iran Beachhead Lane
nodes.rationale: UAE scores ≈4.1 weighted on freight proximity, forwarder maturity, payment feasibility and customs reliability. Turkey is the strong #2 and lane 2; Germany and the UK justify themselves only as value-dense catalog extensions because rate per kg dominates.

nodes.label: Scaffold Price-Guard Demo Path
nodes.rationale: The demo deliberately exercises the branch where the marketplace price jumps above tolerance: the order moves to PRICE_CHANGED and only continues to PURCHASED after an approved reprice, proving the guard rather than asserting it.

nodes.label: Order State Machine & Transition Table
nodes.rationale: Every transition is an event appended to an immutable order timeline so that tracking, audit and support all read from one source of truth rather than reconstructing history.

nodes.label: POST /admin/orders/{id}/reprice — Approve New Max Procurement Price
nodes.norm_label: post /admin/orders/{id}/reprice — approve new max procurement price

nodes.label: The Five Rules That Shape Everything
nodes.norm_label: the five rules that shape everything

nodes.label: Composition Root as the Only Adapter-Aware Place
nodes.rationale: If swapping an adapter requires touching the core, the change is wrong. Keeping provider names in exactly one file is the enforcement mechanism for the whole ports-and-adapters bet.
nodes.norm_label: composition root as the only adapter-aware place

nodes.label: INVARIANT: Max-Procurement-Price Guard
nodes.rationale: If the live marketplace price at purchase time exceeds the quote's maxProcurementPrice the order branches to PRICE_CHANGED. The guard exists so the system never makes a silent negative-margin purchase; the check is against a live offer immediately before buying.

nodes.label: INVARIANT: Payment ≠ Purchased
nodes.rationale: A successful gateway charge means the customer's money is held; it says nothing about whether the foreign purchase succeeded. Collapsing PAID into PURCHASED is treated as a correctness bug, not a simplification.

nodes.label: ProcurementOrder as a Distinct Aggregate
nodes.rationale: One customer order can split across several marketplaces, so Order and ProcurementOrder must be separate aggregates; every external marketplace order links back to its ProcurementOrder for audit, refunds and reconciliation.

nodes.label: Postgres 17 Service (C collation for stable cursor pagination)
nodes.rationale: POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS forces --locale=C so index ordering stays stable and predictable, which cursor pagination depends on.
nodes.norm_label: postgres 17 service (c collation for stable cursor pagination)

nodes.label: Scaffold Stub Adapters for Every Gated Port
nodes.source_location: Where the gated integrations plug in
nodes.rationale: Zero-dependency stubs (canned Amazon UAE product, fixed FX, always-approve gateway, assisted purchase honouring max-price, canned carrier legs, 10% customs prior) prove the core works before any gate clears; going live means implementing the port and binding it in src/app.ts with nothing in the core changing.
nodes.norm_label: scaffold stub adapters for every gated port

nodes.label: Prototype: Consumer PWA Paste-a-Link Journey
nodes.rationale: A five-step clickable journey (resolve → transparent quote with TTL → OTP → revalidation → pay in Toman → live tracking) rendered in a phone frame, Persian/RTL as it would ship but with English labels kept for review.

nodes.label: Persian-First RTL, Bilingual fa/en Validation Errors
nodes.rationale: Customer-facing strings are Persian and the UI is RTL by default, but validation errors are returned in both fa and en so the client picks — the API never has to guess the caller's locale.
nodes.norm_label: persian-first rtl, bilingual fa/en validation errors

nodes.label: Persian-First Trust & Support AI Layer
nodes.rationale: Strong open-source Persian LLMs are scarce, so production quality requires fine-tuning a base model on Persian plus domain data. Trust is a conversion lever, not just a support cost — proactive milestone narration in Persian differentiates against fragmented Instagram sellers.

nodes.label: DECISION A1: AI as Operating Substrate, Not a Feature
nodes.rationale: The moat is not 'we built the website' — competitors get the same models. AI is treated as the substrate of Product Resolution, Procurement Execution and Customer Trust/Support because the defensible asset is running the lowest-HSPO, highest-STP compliant cross-border operation.
nodes.norm_label: decision a1: ai as operating substrate, not a feature

nodes.label: Deterministic Ledger + LLM Fuzzy Reconciliation Matcher
nodes.rationale: Money is never an LLM decision; the LLM is confined to proposing fuzzy matches between foreign-card descriptors, procurement orders and customer orders, always confirmed by a human or a rule. Target auto-match >99%.
nodes.norm_label: deterministic ledger + llm fuzzy reconciliation matcher

nodes.label: Database-Enforced Append-Only Ledger
nodes.rationale: The Money rule, the transition-table rule and ledger balance are enforced in Postgres via constraints and triggers, not only in application code — an UPDATE against ledger_entry is rejected by the database itself.

nodes.label: Link-First MVP Scope (no catalog/search)
nodes.rationale: A catalog would require merchandising, inventory and discovery surfaces that add no value when the customer already knows the product; one paste-a-link flow collapses the whole product surface to the single job to be done.

nodes.label: Prototype: Admin Exception Queue + Procurement Copilot
nodes.rationale: Operators see only orders that need them, ranked by margin-at-risk × urgency; the copilot prepares everything deterministic (expected vs current price, max authorized) so the human confirms the one irreducible step.
nodes.norm_label: prototype: admin exception queue + procurement copilot

nodes.label: AI Exception Classifier / Ranked Ops Queue
nodes.norm_label: ai exception classifier / ranked ops queue

nodes.label: AI Landed-Cost / Weight Predictor
nodes.rationale: Shipping/customs estimation before warehouse receipt is the largest margin leak, so predicting actual and volumetric weight from title, category, brand and images is the single highest-ROI AI investment; until real receipt data exists, category-level priors plus an explicit risk reserve stand in.

nodes.label: Plan-Follower + Human Confirmation Procurement Pattern
nodes.rationale: Switching browser agents from fully autonomous to plan-follower-with-oversight raised real-world success from ~30% to ~80%; the residual ceiling is auth friction (3DS/OTP), not model capability.

nodes.label: Assisted Procurement with AI Copilot
nodes.rationale: The AI prepares all deterministic context and drives the cart to the pay button; a human confirms only the irreducible step (final purchase / 3DS challenge). Unsupervised browser automation is never the foundation, only an accelerant under a human gate.

nodes.label: The Moat: Compliant Operation + Logistics Data Flywheel
nodes.rationale: Defensibility is neither the AI nor the website. It is a compliant foreign-payment and treasury operation, real logistics data that tightens landed-cost estimates with every delivered order, the lowest HSPO / highest STP procurement, and trust infrastructure. AI is the lever; the operation and the data are the moat.
nodes.norm_label: the moat: compliant operation + logistics data flywheel

nodes.label: RULE: Manage-by-Exception Ops Console
nodes.rationale: Default view is the AI-ranked exception queue (margin-at-risk × urgency), never a list of healthy orders — this is what lets a small operations team run high GMV.

nodes.label: Bug: Money Lost Methods on JSONB Deserialization
nodes.rationale: Money stored in JSONB comes back as a plain object, so hydrateProduct() was added at seven deserialization sites — the practical cost of the value-object invariant crossing a schemaless column.
nodes.norm_label: bug: money lost methods on jsonb deserialization

nodes.label: INVARIANT: Viability Gate at Order Creation
nodes.norm_label: invariant: viability gate at order creation

nodes.label: RULE: Category Allowlist by Density
nodes.rationale: Launch categories are high-value, low-weight, low-volume (electronics, cosmetics/fragrance, watches, jewelry, accessories, non-bulky premium fashion); bulky/heavy/low-value goods wait for a heavy-freight lane.

nodes.label: Logistics Overhead Ratio
nodes.rationale: (international freight + source handling + last-mile + insurance) ÷ product value, with a viability threshold around 25%. Freight scales with chargeable weight = max(actual, volumetric), so overhead rises with distance and weight and falls with product value.

nodes.label: Money Value Object
nodes.rationale: Money is a typed value object {amount, currency}, DB-constrained and never produced by AI, because the ledger must be double-entry and deterministic; floats and implicit currency coercion are the classic source of unrecoverable financial error.

nodes.label: RULE: Consolidation as a Margin Tool
nodes.rationale: Combining chargeable weight and amortizing handling can cut per-parcel cost by up to ~80%, making it the single biggest lever for moving 'weak' orders into 'viable'. It is therefore a first-class product feature with explicit consolidation windows, not a convenience.
nodes.norm_label: rule: consolidation as a margin tool

nodes.label: RULE: Minimum Order Value Gate
nodes.rationale: The quote engine reads the minimum-viable-value cell for the order's route and weight and either blocks the order, suggests consolidation, or nudges toward a cheaper pickup point — rather than quoting a price that is mostly shipping.

nodes.label: RULE: Value-Density Beats Proximity
nodes.rationale: A light, expensive item is viable from far away; a heavy, cheap item is uneconomic even from next door. Therefore the business does not 'support routes' — it gates individual orders on economics and picks the route/model that widens the viable zone.

nodes.label: Prototype: Quote TTL Countdown + Simulated Price Change
nodes.norm_label: prototype: quote ttl countdown + simulated price change

nodes.label: ResolverConfidence Scoring
nodes.rationale: Low-confidence weight/dimension fields route to the pricing risk buffer instead of a hard quote, so an uncertain extraction degrades margin protection rather than silently producing a wrong price.

nodes.label: Universal Adapter / Two-Tier Product Resolver
nodes.rationale: Tier 1 is the official/structured API where available, tier 2 a vision-LLM extraction fallback. This replaces one hand-built brittle scraper per marketplace, so onboarding a new source marketplace takes days rather than sprints, and DOM changes stop breaking resolution.

nodes.label: ResolutionPipeline / Resolution Ladder
nodes.rationale: The ladder is built and tested but no real strategy is registered, because that needs marketplace credentials. Adding the SP-API strategy is one entry in an array in composition/adapters.ts — the seam is the deliverable.

nodes.label: POST /quotes/{id}/refresh — Revalidate Offer, Availability and FX
nodes.norm_label: post /quotes/{id}/refresh — revalidate offer, availability and fx

nodes.label: RULE: Revalidate at Checkout
nodes.rationale: Offer, availability and FX all drift between quote and payment. Refreshing them immediately before the gateway and locking the quote for its TTL is the only way to keep the charged amount and the purchasable amount consistent; it is also the mitigation for AI extraction hallucination (R11).

nodes.label: Failed Attempt: Lifecycle Script Grepping the Shared Worker Log
nodes.rationale: Grepping /tmp/xb-worker.log for order state picked up results from previous runs, making the assertion non-deterministic; replaced by querying the database for the specific order's state.
nodes.norm_label: failed attempt: lifecycle script grepping the shared worker log

nodes.label: RedisSandboxSessionStore (shared API/worker sandbox sessions)
nodes.rationale: Sandbox sessions were in-memory, so the worker process could not see sessions created by the API; moving the store to Redis is what makes a sandbox scenario span both processes.

nodes.label: Redis Service (noeviction, mapped to 6380)
nodes.rationale: maxmemory-policy noeviction is deliberate: this Redis holds single-flight locks and idempotency markers alongside cache entries, and silently evicting a lock under memory pressure would let a cache stampede through. Port 6380 avoids the commonly occupied 6379.

nodes.label: Cache-Aside with Single-Flight and TTL Jitter
nodes.rationale: Third-party reads and expensive joins go through the shared cache package rather than ad-hoc Redis calls, so single-flight stampede protection, TTL jitter and negative caching apply uniformly.
nodes.norm_label: cache-aside with single-flight and ttl jitter

nodes.label: Sandbox Virtual Clock + Seeded Determinism
nodes.rationale: A five-day delivery is walked through in a meeting by pressing +24 hours: nothing sleeps, past shipment legs become visible, and seeded sessions replay identically every time.

nodes.label: Sandbox: Scenario Adapters Behind the Real Ports
nodes.rationale: Nothing gated is live, so the sandbox is how the product is actually demonstrated. It is deliberately not a mock layer beside the real one: sandbox adapters implement the same ports and an X-Sandbox-Session request traverses the same controllers, guards, validation and state machine as production traffic — that is what makes a sandbox run evidence rather than theatre.
nodes.norm_label: sandbox: scenario adapters behind the real ports

nodes.label: DECISION / GATE / BUILD / RULE Status Markers
nodes.rationale: Markers are load-bearing rather than decorative: DECISION is a locked choice, GATE an external dependency to build interface-first, BUILD work to implement, RULE an enforced business rule. They make it explicit which statements may not be silently overridden.
nodes.norm_label: decision / gate / build / rule status markers

nodes.label: Handoff: Current Build State and Verified Surface
nodes.norm_label: handoff: current build state and verified surface

nodes.label: Phase 0.4 Open GATEs (freight quotes, customs, hub partner, last-mile, legal)
nodes.norm_label: phase 0.4 open gates (freight quotes, customs, hub partner, last-mile, legal)

nodes.label: Deviation 1: No SSR — Static Export + OG Meta Service
nodes.rationale: The blueprint chose SSR purely for Instagram/Telegram link previews. A static export plus a small dedicated OG meta service that serves crawler-facing tags recovers the preview benefit without running a Node runtime for the app itself.
nodes.norm_label: deviation 1: no ssr — static export + og meta service

nodes.label: MinIO Service + Bucket Init (xb-packages, xb-documents)
nodes.rationale: Both buckets are explicitly set to anonymous access 'none' at init, so package photos and customs documents are never publicly readable by default.

nodes.label: Async Workers (FX refresh, procurement, tracking, recon)
nodes.norm_label: async workers (fx refresh, procurement, tracking, recon)

nodes.label: Bounded Contexts and Public Domain Events
nodes.norm_label: bounded contexts and public domain events

nodes.label: Deviation 2: RabbitMQ, Not BullMQ
nodes.rationale: RabbitMQ gives a real dead-letter topology, per-queue routing and backoff exchanges that BullMQ-on-Redis does not. Redis stays, but only for cache and the FX snapshot — never as a queue.

nodes.label: Transactional Outbox + Event-Only Cross-Module Communication
nodes.rationale: Domain events are written to the outbox in the same transaction as the state change and then relayed to RabbitMQ. Events cross module boundaries and direct cross-module calls do not — this is precisely what makes later extraction into services possible.

nodes.label: Pending Real Integrations Behind PaymentPort / ProcurementPort / LogisticsPort
nodes.norm_label: pending real integrations behind paymentport / procurementport / logisticsport

nodes.label: Model B: PUDO / Pickup-Point Network
nodes.rationale: Out-of-home delivery is roughly 25% cheaper than home delivery and cuts returns cost by up to 60%, so skipping the door last-mile is what turns a bulky low-value order from weak into viable. Added as a phase-2 delivery option using partner shops before any lockers.

nodes.label: Model D: Hawala-Style 'Goods Gate' Agent Network
nodes.rationale: Borrows hawala's decoupling of delivery from settlement so a destination agent holding stock can deliver instantly while replenishment flows asynchronously. Scored 2/5 as a general model but 4/5 as a narrow instant-delivery feature for pre-stocked hero SKUs, because the moment agents settle cross-border cash imbalances it becomes an unlicensed informal value-transfer system.
nodes.norm_label: model d: hawala-style 'goods gate' agent network

nodes.label: Deliberately Unbuilt Seams (real adapters, merchant panel, WS, recon)
nodes.rationale: Each unbuilt item has a designed seam and no implementation so it can be added without reworking what exists; password hashing is SHA-256 only to match the dev seed and must move to argon2id before production.
nodes.norm_label: deliberately unbuilt seams (real adapters, merchant panel, ws, recon)

nodes.label: Three Exogenous Gates (payment, customs, compliance)
nodes.rationale: AI upgrades everything inside the four walls but changes nothing about foreign-payment banking, customs/importability and legal compliance. These remain the true GO/NO-GO determinants and must not be papered over by AI optimism.

nodes.label: RULE: Goods Only, Never Cross-Border Value Transfer
nodes.rationale: Hawala-style value transfer is regulated money transmission and illegal unlicensed. Agents may only ever touch goods, settlement stays inside each jurisdiction, customs are declared properly, personal-import limits are enforced on travelers, and a full audit trail is kept.
nodes.norm_label: rule: goods only, never cross-border value transfer

nodes.label: Compliance Gate (master switch)
nodes.rationale: No architecture path may depend on concealment, account sharing, or bypassing marketplace/AML controls. AI cannot substitute for legal validation, so compliance stays the master switch before production regardless of technical readiness.
